lessons.title: پانی (pānī) — "water," and لینا put back to work
lessons.gloss: water — the first word you would actually ask for, and a verb from three chapters ago put back to work

segments.text: Say merā dil — my heart, closing the body words, and recall that its PIE root reached Urdu by the Persian road while the same root reached Sanskrit's hṛdaya by a different one. This chapter turns to the four things you would actually ask for. لینا, "to take," from three chapters back, gets its first real use since it was taught.

blocks.title: You'll want to know first — one word

segments.text: پانی — pānī — water.
پانی (pānī) is masculine.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: naming what you'd take

segments.text: میں پانی لیتا ہوں۔ — maiṅ pānī letā hūṅ. — I take/get water (man speaking). میں پانی لیتی ہوں۔ — maiṅ pānī letī hūṅ. — I take/get water (woman speaking).
لینا's stem le- slots a noun in front of it the same way any transitive verb does. You already hold the whole verb; پانی (pānī) is the first noun you have had to put in front of it.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart — a drink-word, not a water-word

segments.text: pānī continues Sanskrit pānīya, "water, drink," built on pā-, "to drink," from Proto-Indo-European peh₃-. English water is unrelated — it comes from an entirely different PIE root. But peh₃- itself did reach English, by a different door: Latin potare, "to drink," gave English potion and, by way of a sense narrowed to "a poisoned drink," poison. پانی is, underneath, "the drinkable thing" — the same idea English kept for what you drink, not for the substance itself.

segments.instruction: maiṅ pānī letā hūṅ, then maiṅ pānī letī hūṅ
segments.source: [YOU SAY: **maiṅ pānī letā hūṅ**, then **maiṅ pānī letī hūṅ**]

segments.instruction: pānī from pā- becomes Latin potare becomes English potion, poison — not water

segments.text: Is پانی (pānī) related to English water? (No.) Name two English words that do share its root. (Potion and poison.) Say "I take/get water," once as a man would, once as a woman would.
Sources: Wiktionary: پانی (pānī).

lessons.title: چائے (chāy) — "tea," which walked to Urdu rather than sailed
lessons.gloss: tea — Persian again, this time by an overland road from Chinese, and the hamza-ye letter's second word

needs: your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called The letters in this word until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: Say merā pānī — my water, underneath just "the drinkable thing." Here is the drink you would politely ask for right after it, and a letter from Chapter 9 makes a second appearance.

blocks.title: You'll want to know first — one word

segments.text: چائے — chāy — tea.
میری چائے۔ — merī chāy. — "my tea."
چائے (chāy) is feminine.

From the right edge: چ ch, already yours from sochnā and samajhnā; then ا long ā; then ئ, hamza-ye, the vowel-glide letter بھائی introduced; then ے, broad final e from kaise. چائے (chāy)'s ئ does the same job it did in بھائی: keeping ā and the vowel after it from colliding.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart — the same road as خدا and حافظ (hāfiz)

segments.text: چائے is borrowed from Classical Persian چای (chāy), which traces back to Northern Chinese chá, carried overland through Central Asia into Persian before Urdu ever had it. That is the same road خدا and دل travelled in earlier chapters — Persian into Urdu — just with a Chinese starting point this time instead of one further west.

Tea that instead reached Europe by sea kept a different form, from southern coastal Chinese, which is why English says tea and French says thé instead of chai. One drink, two words, sorted by whether it travelled by land or by water.

segments.instruction: the hamza-ye letter's two words so far — bhāī, chāy
segments.source: [YOU NAME: the hamza-ye letter's two words so far — **bhāī**, **chāy**]

segments.text: Which three languages did چائے (chāy) pass through, in order? (Chinese, then Persian, then Urdu.) Why does English say "tea" instead of "chai"? (It arrived by sea, carrying a different Chinese form.) Which earlier Urdu word already used the hamza-ye letter? (بھائی.)
Sources: Wiktionary: چائے (chāy).

lessons.title: دودھ (dūdh) — "milk," and a false friend worth naming before you fall for it
lessons.gloss: milk — a sixth letter learns to breathe, and an English cousin that is NOT the word you'd guess

needs: your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called The letters in this word until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: Say merī chāy — my tea, which walked overland from China through Persian before reaching Urdu. This word is what turns it milky, and it hands the two-eyed ھ a sixth letter to aspirate.

blocks.title: You'll want to know first — one word

segments.text: دودھ — dūdh — milk.
میرا دودھ۔ — merā dūdh. — "my milk."
دودھ (dūdh) is masculine.
From the right edge: د d, then و carrying long ū, then د again, then ھ. دھ extends the two-eyed he to a sixth base letter: it has now aspirated ج، ٹ، ڑ، چ، ک, and here it aspirates د, giving dh.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart — the cousin you'd guess wrong

segments.text: dūdh continues Sanskrit dugdhá, literally "milked," from Proto-Indo-European dʰewgʰ-, "to be fit, to yield, to produce." That root also gives Sanskrit duh-, "to milk" — the verb sitting directly under this noun.

Here is the trap. English dough looks like the obvious match, and it is not: dough comes from a completely different PIE root, dʰeigʰ-, "to knead, to form" — the root behind the shape of bread, not the substance of milk. The real English cousin of دودھ (dūdh) is a quieter word: doughty, "brave, capable," from the very same dʰewgʰ-, "fit for, of use." A doughty person and milked milk share an ancestor; bread dough does not.

segments.instruction: six letters now carrying ھ — ج، ٹ، ڑ، چ، ک، د

segments.instruction: دودھ (dūdh) is NOT related to English dough
segments.source: [YOU REJECT: **دودھ** is NOT related to English **dough**]

segments.instruction: دودھ (dūdh) from dʰewgʰ- becomes English doughty, the real cousin

segments.text: Which English word looks like a match for دودھ (dūdh) but is not one? (Dough.) Which English word actually is the cousin? (Doughty.) What Sanskrit verb sits directly under دودھ (dūdh)? (duh-, "to milk.")
Sources: Wiktionary: دودھ (dūdh); Etymonline: doughty.

segments.prompt: Which English word is the REAL cousin of دودھ (dūdh) — dough, or doughty?

feedback.correct: Right: doughty, from dʰewgʰ-. Dough is from an unrelated root, dʰeigʰ-.
feedback.incorrect: It's doughty, not dough — dough comes from a different, unrelated PIE root.

lessons.title: روٹی (roṭī) — "bread," and پسند closes the chapter
lessons.gloss: bread — an honest dead end, and پسند put back to work on everything this chapter taught

segments.text: Three drinks so far: pānī, chāy, dūdh — and recall دودھ's real English cousin was doughty, not the tempting dough. This chapter's fourth and final word is the one you would eat, not drink.

blocks.title: You'll want to know first — one word

segments.text: روٹی — roṭī — bread.
میری روٹی۔ — merī roṭī. — "my bread."
روٹی (roṭī) is feminine.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart — another honest dead end

segments.text: roṭī continues Sauraseni Prakrit roṭṭa-, from Sanskrit roṭikā, "a kind of bread." That word is built inside Sanskrit itself, on a root meaning "to strike, to crush" — the pounding and rolling that turns grain into flatbread. The trail stops there: no proposed Proto-Indo-European ancestor, no English cousin. کان and پڑھنا hit the same honest wall earlier in this book. Not every word gets a Greek or Latin relative, and saying so plainly is better than inventing one.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: مجھے... پسند ہے, one more time

segments.text: مجھے روٹی پسند ہے۔ — mujhe roṭī pasand hai. — I like bread.

The dative-experiencer frame from Chapter 8 was built for -nā infinitives — paṛhnā, likhnā. It works just as well for a plain noun: whatever pleases you sits in the subject slot, and ہے agrees with it, not with you.

segments.instruction: mujhe roṭī pasand hai, then swap in pānī, then dūdh
segments.source: [YOU SAY: **mujhe roṭī pasand hai**, then swap in **pānī**, then **dūdh**]

all four foods with merā or merī correctly chosen

segments.text: Does روٹی (roṭī) have a secure English cousin? (No — the trail stops at Sanskrit.) Of this chapter's four foods, which one is the Persian loan? (چائے (chāy).) Say "I like bread" using the frame from Chapter 8.
Sources: Wiktionary: روٹی (roṭī).

segments.prompt: Type the Urdu sentence 'I like bread.'
